7 **issuing division:** engineering standards division **issue date:** 75-06-01 (pce) / 2117-06-01 (ce) **supersedes:** ci-es-2204 rev.
6 (72-03-15 pce) --- ## 1.
system overview the haven island floodwall system comprises a series of nested retaining wall sections, drainage channels, and retaining tanks maintained under cyanite industries' exclusive engineering authority as mandated by the clairos governance council.
the high-capacity pump assemblies addressed by this standard are the primary active components of the floodwall's water management function, responsible for continuous transfer of accumulated retaining-tank water back through the outer barrier channels and into the open ocean.
secondary reverse osmosis processing is co-located at pump assembly stations as specified in companion standard ci-es-2211.
this standard governs maintenance, inspection, part replacement, and emergency operational procedures for all primary pump assemblies installed across floodwall sections.
adherence is mandatory for all engineering division personnel and any contracted maintenance teams operating under cyanite industries authorization.
**1.1 scope** this standard applies to all primary pump assemblies currently installed in haven floodwall sections as enumerated in the floodwall infrastructure register (ci-reg-0044, current revision).
section configurations vary by physical length of the floodwall segment; accordingly, each floodwall section contains between 12 and 18 primary pump assemblies depending on section length.
all pump assemblies within scope are powered by the nuclear fission reactor grid serving the northern floodwall stations, as documented in ci-es-1100 (nuclear power distribution — floodwall).
component specifications ### 2.1 primary pump assembly — configuration summary | component | specification | notes | |-----------|--------------|-------| | pump casing | grade ci-7 marine alloy | saltwater-rated exterior coating | | drive motor | 4.2 mw induction motor | reactor-grid direct supply | | impeller assembly | ci-imp-440 series | see section 2.2 | | bearing housing | sealed double-row, ci-brg-14 | grease-packed, sealed | | inlet valve assembly | pneumatic actuated, 900mm bore | ci-vlv-09a or ci-vlv-09b | | outlet manifold | cast ci-7 alloy, flanged | connects to primary discharge channel | ### 2.2 impeller specifications and service life the ci-imp-440 series impeller is the primary wear component of each pump assembly.
impellers are precision-cast for resistance to cavitation and long-term saltwater exposure.
the following specifications govern impeller installation, monitoring, and replacement: **rated operational life:** the ci-imp-440 impeller carries a rated operational life of **4,200 hours** of continuous or cumulative active pumping operation before mandatory replacement is required.
this limit is not advisory; operation beyond 4,200 hours constitutes a breach of this standard and voids cyanite industries' infrastructure liability coverage for the affected section.
**cumulative hour tracking:** each impeller must be tagged at installation with a ci-asset label carrying a unique serial identifier.
operational hours are logged by the section's pump management controller and must be manually cross-verified during each scheduled inspection (see section 3).
**replacement parts — manufacturing source:** replacement impellers for all floodwall pump assemblies are manufactured **exclusively at the sarento fabrication facility**.
no substitute supplier is approved under this standard.
requisitions must be submitted through the ci logistics chain referencing part number ci-imp-440 and the relevant section's infrastructure register code.
standard lead time from sarento to haven delivery is 14–21 working days; emergency fabrication lead time is 5–7 working days subject to sarento production scheduling.
section engineers are required to maintain a minimum on-hand impeller stock as specified in appendix a (minimum inventory requirements by section).
inspection schedule ### 3.1 scheduled full inspection intervals all primary pump assemblies must undergo a **full inspection every 180 days** (approximately 6 months).
no extension of this interval is permitted under any operational circumstances except as authorized in writing by the director of floodwall engineering operations under the emergency deferral process (ci-proc-0089), which requires concurrent notification to the cgc infrastructure liaison.
deferral is limited to a maximum of 14 additional days in any single instance.
the table below summarizes the inspection cadence and the principal activities performed at each interval: | inspection type | interval | principal activities | |----------------|----------|---------------------| | full inspection | every 180 days | see section 3.2 | | intermediate check | every 30 days | visual inspection, vibration log review, operational hour tally | | post-emergency check | within 24 hours of bypass activation | see section 5.3 | ### 3.2 full inspection — required activities full inspections must be performed by a minimum of two ci-certified pump engineers and must include the following activities, completed in sequence: 1.
isolation of the pump assembly from the active pumping circuit per ci-proc-0022 (pump isolation lockout/tagout).
physical inspection of impeller assembly: measurement of blade wear profile against ci-dim-440 reference gauge; recording of cumulative operational hours from pump management controller.
bearing housing inspection: disassembly, visual inspection of bearing surfaces, re-greasing or replacement per ci-es-2204 appendix b criteria.
inlet valve actuator test: full open/close cycle with pressure measurement.
outlet manifold seal integrity check.
pump casing inspection for corrosion breach, weld integrity, and coating degradation.
drive motor electrical inspection per companion standard ci-es-0880.
return to service verification: full-load pump test not less than 30 minutes before removal of lockout/tagout.
### 3.3 maintenance service-life cross-reference engineers scheduling impeller replacements should note the relationship between the impeller's rated operational life and the full inspection interval.
the rated operational life of the ci-imp-440 impeller is **4,200 hours**, while the mandatory full inspection interval is **180 days** (equivalent to approximately 4,320 hours of elapsed calendar time).
impeller cumulative operational hours must therefore be tracked and reported at every full inspection; an impeller running at or near continuous full capacity may approach or reach its mandatory replacement threshold within a single inspection cycle.
section engineers are responsible for ensuring replacement stock is available before cumulative hours approach the 4,200-hour limit.
see appendix a for stock requirements.
maintenance constraints ### 4.1 simultaneous offline pump limit continuous floodwall operation requires that pumping capacity remain within safe operational margins at all times.
to ensure section-level hydraulic redundancy is maintained during maintenance activities, **no more than 2 pump assemblies per section may be offline simultaneously for maintenance, inspection, or replacement at any given time**.
this limit of 2 concurrent offline units is absolute and applies regardless of section size, seasonal water ingress rates, or maintenance backlog conditions.
personnel scheduling maintenance activities must verify current offline status of all pump assemblies within a section before initiating any isolation procedure.
if 2 assemblies are already offline, no additional isolation may be initiated until at least one offline assembly is returned to service and confirmed operational.
this restriction applies to both planned maintenance and unplanned replacement activities.
> **⚠ safety warning — ci-w-044:** any attempt to bring a third pump assembly offline in a section where 2 are already offline constitutes a safety-critical protocol violation.
the section supervisor must be notified immediately.
if operational necessity appears to require exceeding this limit (e.g., simultaneous impeller failure in multiple assemblies), the emergency bypass procedure in section 5 must be activated and the cgc infrastructure liaison notified within 1 hour.
### 4.2 scheduling constraints full inspection scheduling must be coordinated across sections to prevent simultaneous high-maintenance-load periods in adjacent sections.
section engineers must submit quarterly maintenance schedules to the floodwall operations coordination centre (ci-focc) no later than 30 days before each quarter.
ci-focc maintains a system-wide pump availability dashboard and will flag schedule conflicts before authorization is granted.
emergency bypass procedures ### 5.1 bypass system overview each pump assembly is equipped with a motorized bypass valve connecting its inlet line to the secondary retaining channel network.
**emergency bypass mode allows water to be redirected to secondary retaining channels if a pump fails mid-cycle**, preventing uncontrolled backflow into the primary retaining tanks while the failed assembly is isolated and assessed.
activation of emergency bypass mode is a controlled procedure and does not require pump isolation lockout; the bypass valve and the pump circuit operate in parallel configurations during transition.
### 5.2 bypass activation sequence 1.
identify failed assembly via pump management controller alarm or manual observation.
confirm failure type: complete motor trip, impeller seizure, or inlet valve failure.
activate bypass valve via local panel control or remote ci-focc command.
confirm secondary retaining channel flow on section hydraulic display.
isolate failed assembly inlet valve.
notify ci-focc of bypass activation within 15 minutes; initiate post-emergency check within 24 hours per section 3.1.
### 5.3 post-emergency check requirements following any bypass activation, the affected pump assembly must undergo a full post-emergency inspection before being returned to service.
this inspection follows the full inspection checklist in section 3.2, with additional focus on impeller and bearing damage assessment as specified in ci-es-2204 appendix c (post-failure impeller damage classification).
if the impeller's cumulative operational hours are within 500 hours of the 4,200-hour rated life, mandatory replacement is required regardless of visual condition.
supply chain notes **6.1 impeller lead times and stock requirements** as specified in section 2.2, all ci-imp-440 replacement impellers are manufactured exclusively at the sarento fabrication facility.
given the 14–21 working day standard lead time, section engineers must monitor cumulative impeller hours proactively.
minimum on-hand stock levels by section size are tabulated in appendix a.
sections with sections containing 16 or more pump assemblies are classified as high-density sections and carry elevated minimum stock requirements.
**6.2 requisition authorization** impeller requisitions with a unit cost exceeding 50,000 phi credits require countersignature from the floodwall operations director.
emergency fabrication requisitions must be authorized by the director and copied to the ci sarento logistics liaison within 2 hours of submission.
**6.3 approved parts list** no substitution of non-ci-sourced components is permitted in any primary pump assembly.
any non-standard component installed in a floodwall pump assembly must be removed and replaced with the approved ci part within 72 hours of discovery.
incidents involving non-approved components must be reported to the engineering standards division under ci-proc-0101.

questions regarding interpretation of this standard should be directed to the floodwall operations coordination centre.
this document is classified yellow and is approved for distribution to all cyanite industries engineering division personnel and authorized cgc infrastructure contractors.* *ci-es-2204 rev.

the collapse, following identical outcomes in 2117 and 2118, has deepened concerns among trade analysts that the review process itself may be approaching irrelevance.
the review convened on 20 june at the hegemony council hall, with cgc and bloc delegations formally seated on the morning of opening day.
atmosphere in the early sessions was described by attending correspondents as cautiously professional — markedly cooler than the 2118 review, which at least opened with a joint statement of intent before unraveling.
this year, no such statement was issued.
--- ## the cgc proposal the central cgc offer arrived on day two, when the cgc trade delegation presented a tariff reduction framework for aquaculture products: a reduction in the existing tariff rate from 14 percent down to 9 percent, conditional upon bloc-wide adoption of cgc-standard quality certification protocols across all relevant export categories.
by the standards of the past several review cycles, the offer was considered substantive.
"we came here with a real concession on the table," said the cgc's lead trade representative in remarks to the assembled delegations.
"a five-point reduction in the aquaculture tariff represents meaningful economic relief for the bloc's largest export sector.
the certification alignment we are requesting is standard practice across every major trading zone in which cgc members operate." the offer was intended, according to sources familiar with the cgc's internal preparation, to drive a wedge between bloc members by targeting the economic interests of zonnon — whose aquaculture export economy is the most directly affected by the existing tariff structure — while presenting the certification requirement as a technical rather than political demand.
--- ## zonnon's rejection the strategy did not survive contact with the zonnon delegation.
within hours of the cgc's formal presentation, zonnon's lead negotiator delivered a statement that left no room for procedural maneuvering.
the cgc's quality certification requirement, the delegation said, was "a regulatory trojan horse" — language that was prepared, not improvised, and clearly designed for public circulation.
"we have seen this mechanism deployed against smaller governments before the cascade," the zonnon statement continued.
"you accept the technical standard.
the technical standard expands.
you wake up five years later administering your export economy under cgc regulatory framework.
we will not be doing that." zonnon's isolationist-aligned negotiating bloc has consistently taken the harder line in review proceedings, and their characterization of the certification requirement rapidly became the dominant framing among bloc-aligned observers.
--- ## kashikari's position kashikari's response, by contrast, was initially more measured.
on day two, following the cgc presentation, members of the hegemony delegation were observed in extended sidebar conversation with their cgc counterparts — a procedural signal that in prior years has presaged formal counter-proposals.
one senior hegemony trade official, speaking without attribution, acknowledged that "the arithmetic of a five-point reduction is not nothing, and the council is obligated to examine it on its merits." by day three, however, kashikari had publicly withdrawn any indication of interest in the cgc proposal.
the reversal followed intensive consultations between the kashikari and zonnon delegations on the evening of day two, the details of which have not been disclosed.
kashikari's formal statement on day three aligned closely with zonnon's framing, describing the certification requirement as "a condition requiring further legal examination" and indicating that kashikari "cannot in the current session proceed on the basis of the proposal as structured." --- ## nyari's delayed arrival nyari's delegation was not present for the opening two days of review.
the confederation's federal council, whose supermajority consensus requirement governs external negotiating authorizations, did not complete its authorization process in time for the nyari delegates to depart by the review's opening date.
the delegation arrived on day three — not, as some early reports suggested, in protest or by choice, but because the federal council's deliberative process had not concluded.
nyari's lead delegate confirmed this directly upon arrival: "we have been authorized to observe and consult.
we were not authorized to be here sooner." the late arrival substantially constrained nyari's role in the proceedings.
by the time their delegation was seated, the key exchanges between the cgc, zonnon, and kashikari had already occurred, and the review's trajectory was largely set.
--- ## final collapse and historical pattern days four and five produced no new substantive proposals from any party.
the cgc declined to withdraw the certification condition; the bloc delegations declined to accept it.
on 24 june, the review was formally adjourned without agreement and without a scheduled resumption date.
the 2119 failure marks the third consecutive year the annual review has produced no binding outcome — following the collapses of 2117 and 2118, each of which ended under different immediate circumstances but with identical results.
asked whether a fourth consecutive failure would prompt a structural review of the process itself, the cgc's delegation offered no response.
several bloc trade officials, speaking informally after adjournment, suggested that the review's value may now be more symbolic than practical.
"the question," one said, "is whether symbolism is still worth five days in cape tidak." *danya korrel covers bloc affairs for the sharpsea maritime herald.
she reported on the 2118 review and the 2117 preliminary talks.* # incident report ir-77-0087 ## nanobot containment breach — west haven port terminal 6 **issuing authority:** tec environmental compliance unit **classification:** l4 — restricted internal **report date:** 77-02-19 **incident date:** 77-02-14 **incident reference:** ir-77-0087 --- ## 1.
incident summary at 03:17 local time on 77-02-14, an electromagnetic filtration barrier at west haven port terminal 6 lost power during a scheduled one network enterprises cargo loading operation.
the barrier failure permitted an estimated 1.2 billion nanobots to escape haven aboard three outbound cargo vessels before barrier function was restored at 05:42.
this report documents the timeline of the incident, its root cause, assessed impact, classification rationale, stakeholder responses received, and corrective actions proposed.
terminal 6 is a significant node in one network enterprises' outbound logistics chain, handling approximately 18% of all one outbound cargo from west haven.
the incident therefore affected a material volume of haven-departing freight during the window of barrier inoperability.
timeline of events | time (local) | event | |---|---| | 02:45 | primary power supply for terminal 6 filtration array taken offline for scheduled maintenance by tec infrastructure services.
| | 02:47 | backup power supply unit assessed as active by on-duty technician.
secondary activation protocol logged as complete.
| | 03:17 | capacitor failure in backup power supply unit causes total loss of barrier function.
filtration barrier enters unpowered state.
alarm triggered at tec environmental compliance monitoring station.
| | 03:22 | on-call environmental compliance officer notified.
cargo loading operations at terminal 6 not immediately suspended pending confirmation of alarm source.
| | 03:51 | tec infrastructure services confirms barrier inoperability.
one cargo loading operations notified and suspended.
| | 05:42 | electromagnetic filtration barrier restored to full operational function following emergency capacitor replacement.
| the barrier remained inoperative for approximately 2 hours and 25 minutes from initial failure.
during the window between 03:17 and 05:42, an estimated 1.2 billion nanobots were carried beyond the haven filtration perimeter aboard three outbound one network enterprises cargo vessels.
root cause analysis investigation by tec environmental compliance unit has identified the following primary causal chain: **primary cause:** the terminal 6 filtration array's primary power supply was taken offline for scheduled maintenance at 02:45.
in accordance with standard protocol, this action required confirmation that the backup power supply unit was fully active and load-bearing before primary supply disconnection.
on-duty technician logs indicate the secondary activation protocol was recorded as complete; however, post-incident inspection reveals that a capacitor within the backup power supply unit had developed a pre-failure stress fracture not detectable under standard pre-maintenance inspection procedures.
when the backup unit assumed load at 02:47, the fractured capacitor sustained function for approximately 30 minutes before failing catastrophically at 03:17, causing total barrier power loss.
**contributing factor:** the 34-minute delay between initial alarm activation (03:17) and suspension of one cargo loading operations (03:51) allowed continued cargo transit through the inoperative barrier zone, increasing total nanobot egress volume during the incident window.
**no evidence** was found of deliberate interference, system tampering, or systemic failure extending beyond the identified capacitor fault.
impact assessment an estimated 1.2 billion nanobots are assessed to have exited haven perimeter containment aboard three one network enterprises outbound cargo vessels during the period of barrier inoperability.
distribution across the three vessels is estimated but not confirmed; cargo manifests for all three vessels have been logged for reference.
nanobots operating beyond haven's relay coverage infrastructure are assessed to enter full dormancy within 14 hours of perimeter departure, at which point they present no active operational capability.
tec technical assessments confirm that dormant nanobots in open maritime environments do not exhibit behavioral propagation, data relay function, or autonomous activity.
the 18% share of one outbound cargo ordinarily processed through terminal 6 indicates that nanobot carriage beyond haven perimeter on outbound vessels is a pre-existing baseline phenomenon at low levels under normal operating conditions.
the terminal 6 incident produced egress significantly in excess of normal leakage levels during the 03:17–05:42 window.
classification **severity level: 3 — significant but contained.** this classification was issued by tec environmental compliance, the responsible regulatory authority for nanobot perimeter integrity at haven port facilities.
no other regulatory body holds authority to issue or modify this classification.
the severity level 3 designation reflects the following assessment: the egress volume substantially exceeded normal operational baseline; however, dormancy onset within 14 hours of relay coverage loss materially limits the potential for ongoing impact.
no evidence of reception, recovery, or intentional diversion of escaped nanobot populations has been identified.
the incident is therefore assessed as significant in scope but bounded in consequence.
stakeholder response **one network enterprises** filed a formal objection to this incident characterization on 77-02-17, asserting that tec's filtration maintenance scheduling practices were negligent and that the delay in suspending cargo loading operations following alarm activation compounded preventable egress volume.
one's objection is noted in this report.
tec environmental compliance acknowledges that the 34-minute loading continuation window is a procedural point warranting review; however, the characterization of maintenance scheduling as negligent is not accepted.
the capacitor failure was not detectable under applicable pre-maintenance inspection standards.
one's objection is filed with this report as annex a and will be transmitted to tec's legal compliance division for formal response.
corrective actions the following corrective measures are proposed for implementation within 45 days of this report's issuance: 1.
**backup power redundancy:** all filtration array backup power supply units at haven port terminals to undergo enhanced capacitor stress-fracture inspection, extending current pre-maintenance inspection procedures to include non-destructive material fatigue assessment.
tec infrastructure services to propose revised inspection protocol within 15 days.
**secondary redundancy layer:** engineering review to assess feasibility of installing a tertiary backup power unit at all severity-zone filtration arrays, such that a single backup unit failure does not produce total barrier inoperability.
**cargo loading suspension protocol:** standard operating procedure to be revised to require immediate suspension of all cargo loading operations at affected terminals upon barrier alarm activation, pending physical confirmation of barrier status, rather than pending confirmation of alarm source.
revised protocol to be circulated to all port terminal operations liaisons, including one network enterprises terminal 6 operations management.
**capacitor replacement cycle:** scheduled replacement cycle for filtration array backup supply capacitors to be reviewed; current cycle intervals to be assessed against observed failure characteristics.

analysis draws on signals intelligence, maritime monitoring data, and interagency reporting from bloc partner nations.
the period under primary review is 2114 to the date of this document, with particular attention to developments in the first half of 2117 ce.
the cgc's coercive strategy appears increasingly deliberate and multi-vector in character, coordinating external trade pressure with internal political destabilization rather than relying on either mechanism in isolation.
--- ### section ii — economic coercion vectors #### ii.a — tariff and sanctions pressure cgc-aligned commercial entities have in 2116 and 2117 progressively expanded the application of informal non-tariff barriers against zonnon-origin aquaculture exports to haven.
these measures, applied through licensing delays at haven's west haven port authority rather than via formal cgc resolution, are designed to impose economic friction while preserving plausible deniability.
formal cgc sanction resolutions remain absent, likely reflecting the deadlock within the council rather than any restraint of intent.
this division assesses that formal sanction instruments remain a credible escalatory option should cgc internal coordination improve.
#### ii.b — shipping route interdiction maritime data collected by the zonnon naval monitoring station through may 2117 ce confirms that one network enterprises redirected 23% of non-essential shipping away from bloc-adjacent routes between january and may 2117.
the diversion pattern is consistent with deliberate economic isolation rather than commercially motivated rerouting: alternative routes selected by one vessels are in several documented instances operationally longer and costlier, indicating that route selection reflects strategic intent rather than logistical efficiency.
the effect on bloc inter-island commerce has been measurable, with kashikari transit revenues reporting a confirmed 8–11% contraction for the period.
zonnon's own deep-water port traffic at tavenport is down approximately 14% year-on-year through the same window.
this division regards one's routing decisions as the most immediately quantifiable cgc coercive instrument currently active against bloc interests.
#### ii.c — internal influence operations and astroturfing this division has identified seven suspected cgc-funded astroturfing operations within the republic since 2114.
the operations vary substantially in mechanism, target audience, and apparent funding pathway.
two operations focused on amplifying labor grievances within zonnon island's aquaculture sector, seeding disinformation about export revenue misallocation to erode public confidence in the current parliamentary administration.
one operation targeted zonnon's university networks, funding a series of academic events framed as independent policy forums but structured to promote dependency arguments favorable to cgc alignment.
one operation involved the placement of synthetic editorial content in three regional media publications through shell-company advertising intermediaries, promoting narratives of zonnon's economic isolation as self-inflicted.
three of the seven operations targeted the accommodationist political faction directly, providing coordinated financial and logistical support designed to amplify accommodationist calls for trade normalization with haven and to give that faction disproportionate visibility in domestic political coverage.
one operation remains under active investigation; its target and mechanism have not yet been fully characterized.
the breadth of this campaign — spanning economic, academic, media, and direct partisan vectors simultaneously — indicates a degree of operational resourcing inconsistent with opportunistic interference.
this division assesses these operations as a coordinated program rather than discrete unrelated incidents.
--- ### section iii — force posture considerations zonnon's standing naval force comprises approximately 40,000 active personnel, constituting the largest uniformed military capacity within the sharpsea bloc.
the force is structured primarily for coastal defense and counter-interdiction operations consistent with the republic's defensive military doctrine, which treats cgc economic and political destabilization as the primary threat category.
it is the assessment of this division that the current force posture remains appropriate to that doctrine.
the officer corps of the zonnon maritime defense command skews isolationist in political orientation, a fact that must be acknowledged in any honest assessment of how this command's analytical conclusions are likely to be received by accommodationist civilian government elements.
this division notes this structural reality without prejudice and recommends that assessments of this nature be distributed to civilian government counterparts with accompanying methodological documentation to permit independent review.
--- ### section iv — threat level assessment having reviewed all identified coercion vectors in aggregate — tariff friction, confirmed shipping diversion, and a coordinated seven-operation internal influence campaign — this division rates the overall cgc economic coercion threat level as **elevated** on the command's four-tier scale (guarded / moderate / elevated / severe).
the current rating reflects active, measurable harm to zonnon's external trade position and confirmed interference in domestic political processes, without yet crossing thresholds associated with direct economic blockade or military posturing.
--- ### section v — recommendations 1.
this command recommends immediate coordination with nyari confederation signals intelligence services to cross-reference internally identified astroturfing patterns with any corresponding financial or communications data held by nyari.
this command recommends the prime minister's security council formally brief the kashikari hegemony council on the one shipping diversion data, with a view to collective bloc documentation of the pattern for potential external diplomatic use.
this command recommends review of domestic counterintelligence resourcing in light of the identified seven-operation internal influence campaign, with particular attention to academic and media sector vulnerabilities.

scope and applicability 1.1 this document constitutes the authoritative technical reference for cryptographic standard ncc-7, as adopted by the nyari confederation federal council by instrument nfc-res-2112-44 dated 2112-09-01.
1.2 ncc-7 applies mandatorily to: - all inter-island routing infrastructure operated by confederation member councils - all cryptographic services offered to sharpsea bloc partner nations under bilateral or multilateral service agreements - all government communications facilities operating under confederation administrative jurisdiction - all third-party operators holding a confederation cryptographic service authorization (ccsa) for bloc-facing services 1.3 compliance with ncc-7 supersedes compliance with ncc-6 for all covered systems.
operators are required to complete migration to ncc-7 by 2113-03-01.
systems remaining on ncc-6 after this date are considered non-compliant.
1.4 this document does not cover internal intra-island administrative communications below the district-council level.
separate guidance applies (see nfca-int-2112-01).
key parameter summary table | parameter | value | notes | |---|---|---| | asymmetric key length (inter-island routing) | 4096 bits | mandatory minimum | | asymmetric algorithm | ec-nfca-prime or rsa-ncc | see §3.2 | | symmetric session key length | 512 bits | aes-ncc variant | | routing table encryption key length | 256 bits | per-table, per-cycle | | routing table key rotation cycle | 72 hours | fixed; no operator discretion | | maximum inter-island encrypted traffic latency | 340 milliseconds | measured end-to-end, see §5.3 | | minimum ccsa penetration testing duration | 14 days | full continuous regimen | | hardware jurisdiction requirement | new mewan, nyari confederation | see §6 | --- ## 3.
asymmetric key specifications ### 3.1 inter-island routing key pairs 3.1.1 all inter-island routing sessions established under ncc-7 shall use asymmetric key pairs of a minimum length of **4096 bits**.
3.1.2 key pairs shall be generated exclusively on nfca-certified hardware security modules (hsms) meeting the physical specifications described in §6.
key generation on general-purpose computing hardware is not permitted for inter-island routing applications.
3.1.3 public keys shall be distributed through the nyari confederation key registry (nckr), a centrally administered directory operated by the nfca.
key registration requires identity attestation by the operator's council-level authority.
3.1.4 private keys shall not leave the generating hsm at any time.
inter-island session establishment is performed by protocol exchange in which private key material is never transmitted in any form.
3.1.5 key pairs shall have a maximum operational lifespan of 24 months from the date of registration in the nckr.
operators are responsible for initiating key rollover no later than 30 days prior to expiry.
### 3.2 approved asymmetric algorithms 3.2.1 two asymmetric algorithm families are approved for use under ncc-7: - **ec-nfca-prime**: an elliptic curve algorithm over an nfca-designated prime field.
preferred for latency-sensitive applications.
- **rsa-ncc**: rsa with a 4096-bit modulus meeting nfca parameter specifications.
permitted for legacy compatibility with partner-nation systems where ec-nfca-prime is not yet supported.
3.2.2 operators must document algorithm selection rationale in their ccsa application filing.
routing table encryption ### 4.1 rotation requirements 4.1.1 all routing table encryption keys in systems operating under ncc-7 shall rotate on a **72-hour cycle**.
this rotation period is fixed and may not be extended or reduced at operator discretion.
any deviation requires a formal variance request submitted to the nfca, which shall only be granted in documented emergency circumstances.
4.1.2 the 72-hour cycle is measured from the moment of previous key activation, not from the generation event.
operators must ensure that key generation and distribution infrastructure can sustain continuous rotation without gap periods.
4.1.3 routing tables shall be re-encrypted under the new key no later than 15 minutes prior to the expiry of the outgoing key.
systems that fail to complete re-encryption within this window shall treat the routing table as suspended and route traffic through a fallback path (see §4.3).
4.1.4 key rotation events shall be logged to the confederation audit ledger (cal) with a timestamp accurate to within one second.
logs are retained for a minimum of 36 months.
### 4.2 key derivation 4.2.1 routing table encryption keys shall be derived using the nfca-kdf-3 key derivation function from a master seed maintained on nfca-controlled hsms in new mewan.
operators do not hold master seed material.
4.2.2 derived keys are distributed to operator systems through authenticated, encrypted channels using the operator's registered 4096-bit key pair.
### 4.3 fallback routing protocol 4.3.1 in the event of a routing table suspension under §4.1.3, systems shall route traffic exclusively through the confederation emergency routing layer (cerl), which operates on a separate, pre-distributed encrypted routing table valid for up to 6 hours.
4.3.2 cerl activation is automatically reported to the nfca within 30 seconds of initiation.
incidents lasting more than 2 hours require a written incident report submitted within 48 hours of resolution.
traffic latency standards ### 5.1 general principle 5.1.1 ncc-7 is designed to achieve strong cryptographic protection without imposing latency overhead incompatible with operational requirements.
latency thresholds are set based on observed inter-island traffic patterns within the confederation's member island topology.
### 5.2 threshold definition 5.2.1 the maximum allowable latency for inter-island encrypted traffic operating under ncc-7 is **340 milliseconds**, measured end-to-end from packet dispatch at the originating island node to confirmed receipt at the destination island node.
5.2.2 this threshold applies to standard routing traffic.
bulk encrypted transfers operating under separate scheduling protocols (see nfca-blk-2112-03) are governed by different latency standards and are outside the scope of this document.
### 5.3 measurement protocol 5.3.1 latency compliance shall be measured using the nfca distributed latency monitor (dlm), a passive monitoring system co-located with confederation routing nodes.
dlm readings are logged to the cal alongside key rotation events.
5.3.2 operators whose traffic exceeds the 340-millisecond threshold for more than 0.5% of measured traffic in any 30-day period shall submit a latency variance report to the nfca within 14 days of the period close.
hardware jurisdiction and physical security ### 6.1 mandatory hardware jurisdiction 6.1.1 all cryptographic operations performed under ncc-7 — including but not limited to key generation, key derivation, session establishment, routing table re-encryption, and audit log signing — **shall be executed on hardware physically located within new mewan, nyari confederation**, and under the direct physical custody of either the nfca or an nfca-licensed hardware custodian.
6.1.2 remote execution of cryptographic operations on hardware located outside new mewan is not permitted under any circumstance, including emergency or contingency operations.
operators requiring continuity arrangements shall provision redundant new mewan-based hardware rather than geographically distributed alternatives.
6.1.3 the hardware custodian register is maintained by the nfca and is available to authorized bloc-partner administrators upon authenticated request through the nckr portal.
### 6.2 protocol isolation requirements 6.2.1 ncc-7 cryptographic hardware and the software stacks executing on it shall be isolated from external communication protocol layers not explicitly approved by the nfca.
6.2.2 ncc-7 was specifically designed to be **incompatible with tec edge nanobot communication protocols**.
no ncc-7 implementation shall include any protocol translation layer, bridge, or compatibility shim that enables communication with or through edge nanobot signaling infrastructure.
hardware found to contain such components shall be considered non-compliant and shall be decommissioned immediately upon discovery.
6.2.3 protocol isolation compliance is verified during the penetration testing regimen described in §7 and through annual nfca hardware audit.
6.3 physical security minimums 6.3.1 hsms holding key material shall be installed in nfca-rated secure enclaves meeting physical tamper-evidence standard nfca-phy-4 or higher.
tamper-evident seals shall be inspected monthly and after any maintenance event.
certification and authorization ### 7.1 confederation cryptographic service authorization (ccsa) 7.1.1 any operator providing bloc-facing encrypted services — meaning services carrying traffic originating from or destined for entities outside the nyari confederation — is required to hold a valid ccsa issued by the nfca.
7.1.2 ccsa issuance requires the following: (a) submission of a completed ccsa application form (nfca-form-701) including operator identity, system architecture documentation, and algorithm selection rationale (b) hardware inspection by an nfca-designated assessor confirming compliance with §6 (c) satisfactory completion of the penetration testing regimen described in §7.2 (d) execution of an nfca service agreement governing ongoing compliance obligations and audit rights ### 7.2 penetration testing regimen 7.2.1 prior to ccsa issuance, all applicants shall undergo a penetration testing regimen administered by the nfca assurance division or an nfca-approved third-party assessor.
7.2.2 the penetration testing regimen shall span a minimum continuous duration of **14 days**.
testing may not be paused and resumed; any interruption exceeding 4 hours restarts the 14-day period.
7.2.3 the testing scope shall include, at minimum: - asymmetric key exchange attack scenarios - routing table interception and injection attempts - physical interface probing of hsm enclosures - timing-based side-channel analysis - protocol isolation boundary testing (§6.2) - latency-manipulation denial-of-service scenarios 7.2.4 a passing result requires zero critical findings and no more than two moderate findings, with remediation plans accepted by the assessor before ccsa is granted.
7.2.5 ccsa holders are subject to annual re-assessment using an abbreviated 5-day regimen.
a full 14-day regimen is required upon any significant architecture change, defined as modification of key generation hardware, algorithm selection, or routing infrastructure topology.
### 7.3 ccsa duration and renewal 7.3.1 a ccsa is valid for 24 months from the date of issuance.
renewal requires completion of the annual re-assessment and submission of an updated nfca-form-701 no later than 60 days before expiry.
7.3.2 a ccsa that lapses without renewal results in immediate suspension of the operator's nckr key registrations and notification to bloc-partner administrators.

queries regarding interpretation should be directed to the nfca standards office through authenticated channels.
8.2 this document is classified restricted.

prior to founding wto in 71 pce (2113 ce), the author served as a compliance officer at phyrexis group, a tenure that ended when she witnessed and reported internal financial fraud in 70 pce.
she subsequently opted, and has since dedicated her professional efforts to civic advocacy on behalf of the opted community.
her background in corporate regulatory compliance directly informs the evidentiary standards and procedural proposals contained in this paper.
introduction we the opted presents this position paper as a formal statement of our organization's stance on the systematic exclusion of opted havenites from civic participation within the haven island special economic zone.
this is not a paper about the merits or ethics of edge technology itself.
it is a paper about administrative equity: the principle that every havenite, regardless of their relationship to nanobot integration, must retain meaningful access to the civic infrastructure that governs their life.
we the opted was founded in 71 pce by the undersigned, initially as a support and advocacy network for havenites who had chosen to purge edge nanobots from their bodies.
in the years since, our membership has grown to encompass those broadly opposed to the unchecked influence of megacorporate systems over daily havenite life.
as of early 76 pce, wto's membership rolls include approximately 340,000 havenites who are formally registered members and have formally opted — a figure that represents only a fraction of the total opted population across haven.
these 340,000 individuals are the documented base from which the evidence in this paper is drawn.
--- ### ii.
background for most of haven's history, cgc administrative services were delivered through multi-channel access systems: physical offices, text-based digital portals, and, subsequently, edge-integrated interfaces.
opted residents could navigate bureaucratic processes through non-edge channels, experiencing inconvenience but not categorical exclusion.
beginning in 74 pce, the cgc civic services directorate commenced a phased transition of administrative service portals to edge-only interfaces.
this transition, completed across most major service categories by early 75 pce, was presented as a modernization initiative intended to reduce processing backlogs and improve service personalization through nanobot behavioral data integration.
no formal accessibility review was published prior to implementation.
no public comment period was held.
the consequence was predictable and documentable: for havenites who have opted, cgc administrative processes that once required effort now require the biological reintegration of a technology they have deliberately and lawfully chosen to remove from their bodies.
--- ### iii.
evidence of exclusion wto's documentation effort, drawing substantially on senior organizer field research conducted across multiple haven sectors, has catalogued a breadth of administrative exclusion that goes well beyond isolated inconvenience.
the categories of documented harm include: denial of access to medical subsidy recertification portals, requiring opted individuals to present in person at facilities whose in-person intake processes were formally closed during the same transition period; inability to submit occupational licensing renewals for fourteen trades and service categories that moved to edge-verified credential systems in 74 pce; failure to receive mandatory cgc public health notifications distributed exclusively through edge broadcast infrastructure; and, in a particularly acute cluster of cases, denial of access to the haven residential mobility program.
in this last category, wto has documented 14 cases in which opted residents were denied housing relocation permits — not employment permits, not commercial licenses, but housing relocation permits specifically — solely because the application and verification pathway requires active edge-nanobot integration for identity authentication.
in each of these 14 cases, the applicants were otherwise fully qualified and had no adverse administrative history.
the denial in every instance was attributed to system incompatibility, not eligibility failure.
taken together, these exclusions constitute a de facto administrative penalty imposed on any havenite who exercises the lawful choice to remove edge nanobots from their body.
--- ### iv.
legislative proposals we the opted puts forward the following remedies as the minimum necessary standard for civic equity in haven.
**proposal 1 — mandatory parallel access channels.** all cgc administrative services must maintain parallel non-edge access channels capable of delivering every function available through edge-integrated portals.
these channels may be delivered through dedicated physical service offices, text-based secure digital interfaces, or a combination thereof.
no administrative function may be made available exclusively through an edge-dependent pathway.
this requirement should be formalized through a cgc resolution and enforced by the civic services directorate under a public compliance calendar.
**proposal 2 — identity authentication alternatives.** the cgc civic services directorate must develop and deploy at least two edge-independent identity authentication methods across all service categories, within six months of adoption of this proposal.
**proposal 3 — retrospective case review.** all administrative denials issued on the basis of edge-incompatibility since 74 pce should be subject to mandatory review and, where the underlying eligibility criteria are met, reversal.
the 14 documented housing relocation permit denials represent only those cases wto has been able to verify; the actual figure is believed to be substantially higher.
**proposal 4 — accessibility impact assessment.** any future transition of cgc administrative processes to new technological interfaces must be preceded by a published accessibility impact assessment, with a minimum 45-day public comment period before implementation.
conclusion the choice to opt is a lawful exercise of personal autonomy within the haven island special economic zone.
it should not be, and must not become, a disqualification from civic life.
we the opted calls on the cgc to implement the proposals contained in this paper not as a concession to a minority interest, but as a fulfillment of the basic administrative equity that any governance structure owes to the population it claims to serve.
this paper is submitted for public record and will be formally presented to the cgc civic services directorate on 76-04-01.
--- *we the opted — founded 71 pce.
advocating for opted havenites and all those who resist megacorporate overreach.* **renhwa media** **internal memorandum** **classification: confidential** --- **to:** senior leadership team **from:** park soo-hyun, chief executive officer **date:** 73-09-22 **re:** first 90-day strategic review — ceo assessment and preliminary restructuring direction --- this memo summarizes my assessment after ninety days in this role.
i have no interest in softening what i found.
the purpose of this document is to name the problems clearly so that we can begin solving them.
critical problems identified during my first 90 days as ceo, i identified three critical problems requiring immediate structural attention: **operational cost bloat**, **absence of a digital-first content strategy**, and **accelerating talent attrition to competing firms**.
these are not isolated issues.
they are mutually reinforcing, and left unaddressed, any one of them is sufficient to prevent recovery of our market position.
together, they represent an existential risk to this organization.
--- ### ii.
talent attrition the attrition figures are not acceptable.
during the first 90 days of my tenure, renhwa lost **740 employees** — a **6.5% quarterly attrition rate**.
the departures are concentrated in creative production, digital distribution, and mid-level editorial management: precisely the competencies we most need to rebuild.
exit interviews, where conducted, consistently cite three factors — compensation below market rate, absence of a credible growth narrative, and the perception that this organization lacks a viable future.
this perception is not irrational.
it is our job to change the underlying reality, not just the messaging.
immediate action items: compensation benchmarking against current market rates, expedited review of retention packages for critical-path personnel, and a mandatory exit interview protocol for all departures above grade 7.
--- ### iii.
operational cost bloat renhwa's **content production costs are currently 2.3 times the industry average per unit of output**.
i want that figure to sit with everyone reading this memo.
two point three times.
we are producing content at a cost structure appropriate for a dominant market player with locked-in distribution channels.
we are neither of those things.
a significant component of this bloat is our physical production infrastructure in east haven.
our east haven footprint was sized for the organization we were a decade ago.
i am directing an immediate audit of all east haven facility usage, with a target of **reducing our east haven physical footprint by a further 15% by the end of fiscal year 74 pce**.
this is a floor, not a ceiling.
lease renegotiations, consolidations, and where appropriate, full facility exits should all be on the table.
--- ### iv.
digital-first strategy gap renhwa does not have a digital-first content strategy.
we have legacy distribution infrastructure, legacy production workflows, and legacy assumptions about how audiences consume content.
our competitors have spent the last decade building for the formats and channels that actually exist today.
we have spent the last decade defending formats that existed fifteen years ago.
the absence of a credible digital-first strategy is not a secondary concern — it is the structural reason our cost base cannot be justified and our talent cannot be retained.
without a compelling answer to the question of what renhwa is building toward, we cannot recruit, we cannot negotiate from strength, and we cannot make the case for our continued independence.
this is the hardest problem, and it will not be solved in the next quarter.
what we can do in the next quarter is stop pretending we have a plan when we do not, and begin building one honestly.
strategic outlook and preliminary restructuring direction the restructuring plan i am initiating rests on three simultaneous tracks: cost reduction (as outlined above), talent stabilization, and distribution strategy renewal.
on distribution strategy, i want to be direct: organic rebuilding alone will not close the gap in any commercially relevant timeframe.
i have begun preliminary conversations with **three external technology partners**, whose identities i am not disclosing in this memorandum — all three have been described to you here only by sector relevance — including a major immersive platform provider, a logistics-adjacent distribution network, and a data infrastructure firm with content-routing capabilities.
these are early-stage conversations, not commitments.
i raise them here solely to indicate that i am treating external partnership as a necessary component of any realistic recovery path, and that i am actively pursuing options.
the risks are real.
external partnerships constrain editorial autonomy.
they create dependencies.
they will be opposed internally and externally.
i am not unaware of this.
i am also not aware of a costless alternative.
more detail on each track will follow in sector-specific briefings scheduled for the month of 73-10.
--- *park soo-hyun* *chief executive officer, renhwa media* *73-09-22* # kashikari chairperson dismisses haven trade criticism as 'continental thinking' **cape tidak trade forum, kashikari hegemony — 2118-01-09** *danya korrel, bloc affairs correspondent, sharpsea maritime herald* --- cape tidak — the kashikari hegemony's annual cape tidak trade forum opened under grey winter skies on wednesday, drawing delegates from across the sharpsea bloc to the peninsula's distinctive stone-and-steel harbor district.
the forum's centerpiece session, delivered by chairperson maren idako before an audience of shipping executives and intergovernmental representatives, combined a pointed rebuke of cgc criticism with an infrastructure announcement that immediately dominated the day's conversation.
idako, who assumed the hegemony's rotating chair position in 2113 and whose current rotation period runs through early 2118, spoke from the hegemony council hall at the peninsula's midpoint — the building's placement, as ever, a quiet architectural assertion that no single family holds superior standing.
behind her, through the floor-length harbor windows, the cape's deep-water berths were already thick with morning traffic, container vessels queuing beneath cranes whose reach extends well out over the grey-green sharpsea.
"we have heard, again and again, the suggestion from haven that our shipping autonomy is somehow a problem to be solved," idako told the assembled delegates, her remarks measured but blunt.
"that is continental thinking — the assumption that anything beyond their floodwalls is ungoverned space awaiting their management.
the kashikari hegemony has governed these lanes for generations.
we do not require their permission to continue doing so." the line drew sustained applause from the shipping-family delegations occupying the hall's forward rows, where the oldest family compounds — their stone facades visible from the forum's exterior promenade — have anchored the peninsula for more than a century.
--- ## a major infrastructure commitment the forum's headline announcement came midway through idako's address, when she unveiled a **340 million phi credit port modernization program** targeting cape tidak's deep-water harbor.
the program, described as the hegemony's most significant infrastructure investment in over a decade, will fund expansion of the primary commercial quay, deepening of two secondary approach channels to accommodate the next generation of heavy-tonnage vessels, and construction of new cold-storage and logistics coordination facilities on the harbor's eastern breakwater.
"cape tidak is the bloc's commercial spine," idako said.
"this investment ensures it remains that way for the next fifty years, whatever pressures we face from outside." the program is slated to begin procurement tendering within the first quarter of 2118, with principal construction expected to span three years.
--- ## funding questions surface the announcement drew immediate scrutiny from the forum floor over the source of the financing.
in response to questions, chairperson idako identified the backers only as **"private maritime partners"** — a designation she did not elaborate upon, declining to name any specific investors or to characterize whether any portion of the funding originated from entities outside the sharpsea bloc.
when pressed on the point, idako replied that the terms of the investment arrangement were "commercially confidential in the ordinary way" and that full disclosure would follow in hegemony regulatory filings "at the appropriate stage." she did not indicate when that stage would arrive.
the characterization of the backers as "maritime partners" drew pointed commentary in the forum's corridors.
sources familiar with kashikari's financing relationships noted privately that the scale of the commitment — 340 million phi credits — exceeds what any single bloc-internal private consortium has committed to a single harbor project in the post-cascade period.
--- ## zonnon delegation raises concerns in the forum's closing session, a reaction from zonnon's delegation struck a markedly different tone.
zonnon's lead delegate, **ferris ondaal**, speaking on behalf of the republic's trade ministry, offered measured but public criticism of the funding opacity.
"the republic of zonnon congratulates the hegemony on its infrastructure ambitions," ondaal said.
"we would also note, respectfully, that the bloc's credibility as an independent economic actor depends on transparency about who is financing its critical infrastructure.
we would welcome clarification on whether the private funding disclosed today represents any undisclosed entanglement with cgc-aligned entities." ondaal declined to name any specific organization in his remarks, but his delegation's written statement, circulated to press following the session, called for the hegemony to publish the full terms of its investment arrangement prior to the commencement of procurement tendering.
chairperson idako did not respond to ondaal's remarks directly.
a hegemony council spokesperson said only that the program would "proceed in accordance with applicable hegemony regulatory standards." the cape tidak trade forum continues through friday.

--- *end of log — apt-sl-0231-77* *cgc anti-proliferation field team / sarento zone rotation 4* **secret** # cyanite industries ## internal incident report **report number:** ci-76-0419 **classification:** yellow **authoring division:** structural engineering & infrastructure integrity **subject:** structural failure at north haven floodwall retaining tank nr-7 **incident date:** 76-08-01 **report date:** 76-08-03 **author:** structural engineer, northern floodwall maintenance division **distribution:** director of infrastructure operations; north haven site manager; floodwall systems engineering; legal compliance (internal) --- ## section 1 — incident summary retaining tank nr-7, a component of the northern floodwall infrastructure maintained by cyanite industries on the northern shore of haven island, sustained a structural crack of 2.3 meters in length along its interior southeastern wall face.
the defect was identified during a scheduled routine inspection conducted on 76-08-01.
emergency containment and sealing operations were initiated upon confirmation of the finding.
this report documents the discovery timeline, emergency response, root cause analysis, impact assessment, and recommended corrective actions.
--- ## section 2 — discovery timeline **76-08-01, 06:14:** routine scheduled inspection of northern retaining tank array commences per quarterly maintenance cycle.
inspection team: two certified structural inspection technicians and one supervising engineer.
**76-08-01, 09:47:** inspection team identifies anomalous surface discoloration and faint stress fracture pattern on the interior southeastern face of nr-7.
initial visual assessment suggests active crack propagation.
**76-08-01, 10:23:** crack confirmed via ultrasonic thickness gauge and dye penetrant testing.
recorded dimensions: 2.3 meters in length, maximum aperture of 1.4 millimeters at the widest measured point, with an estimated depth penetration of 68% through the tank wall at the deepest section.
site supervisor notified immediately.
**76-08-01, 10:31:** incident formally logged.
north haven site manager notified.
structural emergency protocol initiated under floodwall emergency operations procedure fw-e-004.
--- ## section 3 — emergency response emergency sealing operations were mobilized within 4 hours of the initial discovery of the structural crack.
a containment team was deployed to nr-7 with marine-grade structural epoxy injection equipment and supplementary external bracing assemblies.
given the depth penetration and proximity of nr-7 to the active pump-drain cycle for the northern array, partial rerouting of the drainage load was executed to adjacent tanks nr-6 and nr-8 to reduce hydraulic pressure on the compromised section during repair.
sealing operations proceeded in two stages: primary epoxy injection along the crack profile, followed by external steel patch application and weld sealing at the perimeter.
the full sealing operation was completed 18 hours after the crack's initial discovery.
structural integrity verification testing — including hydrostatic pressure testing at 110% of standard operational load — was conducted immediately following completion and confirmed an adequate temporary seal.
nr-7 remains under elevated monitoring status pending permanent structural remediation (see section 6 — recommendations).
--- ## section 4 — root cause analysis preliminary root cause analysis identifies the primary failure mechanism as progressive corrosion resulting from prolonged saltwater exposure at a previously repaired section of the nr-7 wall.
corrosion indicators — including pitting morphology, oxidation layer composition, and crack propagation geometry — are consistent with galvanic corrosion accelerated by dissimilar metal contact at the 74 pce weld repair zone.
materials analysis of the affected zone, conducted by the internal metallurgical assessment unit on 76-08-02, confirmed that the alloy composition of the repair section installed during the 74 pce scheduled maintenance cycle does not meet cyanite industries' floodwall structural standard ci-fss-12, which specifies a minimum chromium-nickel content for all retaining tank wall materials in constant saltwater contact zones.
the replacement alloy installed in 74 pce falls below this threshold by approximately 14% on chromium content and 9% on nickel content.
procurement records indicate that the substandard alloy was not sourced from an external contractor.
the replacement material was procured and supplied from cyanite industries' own sarento manufacturing operation, through a cost-reduction initiative approved at the sarento manufacturing level in 73–74 pce.
this initiative authorized substitution of non-standard alloy stock for certain secondary infrastructure repair components in order to reduce per-unit materials cost.
the substitution was not flagged against ci-fss-12 compliance requirements at the time of procurement approval, indicating a breakdown in cross-referencing between the cost-reduction program's materials authorization chain and the infrastructure compliance review office.
the corrosion failure is therefore attributable to the interaction of prolonged saltwater exposure — a foreseeable and documented environmental condition for all northern array retaining tanks — with the below-specification alloy material installed during the 74 pce repair.
the failure was not attributable to design error in the original nr-7 construction or to abnormal environmental conditions during the incident period.
--- ## section 5 — impact assessment the incident resulted in no civilian casualties and no flooding of the haven island special economic zone.
the floodwall system's layered redundancy architecture functioned as designed during the emergency period: adjacent retaining tanks absorbed redistributed load without incident, and the pump-drain cycle maintained full operational effectiveness throughout the sealing operation.
the public water supply and reverse osmosis output from the northern array were unaffected.
operational disruption was limited to nr-7 and the immediate maintenance zone.
no evacuation of adjacent north haven sectors was required.
--- ## section 6 — recommendations 1.
**immediate:** conduct full materials compliance audit of all retaining tank repair work completed under the 73–74 pce sarento cost-reduction initiative, cross-referenced against ci-fss-12 and related structural standards.
priority inspection order should prioritize northern array tanks exposed to the highest saltwater contact duration.
**short-term:** initiate permanent structural remediation of nr-7, replacing the compromised wall section with ci-fss-12-compliant alloy material sourced and verified through the standard infrastructure compliance review process.
**procedural:** review and revise the materials authorization chain for cost-reduction procurement initiatives to require mandatory cross-referencing against applicable structural compliance standards prior to approval at any manufacturing level.
**monitoring:** maintain elevated inspection frequency for nr-7 (bi-weekly) until permanent remediation is complete.
